Black prochilodus (Prochilodus nigricans) has a gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 15% [GSI = 15%] during the spawning season when water temperatures reach 24.5 °C [T = 24.5 °C]. This species attains a maximum body length of 45 centimeters [Li = 45 centimeters] as an asymptotic size, based on extensive field surveys across the Amazon basin. The ontogeny of this robust-bodied detritivore begins with the deposition of small, demersal eggs approximately 1 millimeter in diameter. Upon fertilization, the fertilized ovum undergoes rapid cleavage and subsequent embryogenesis within the warm, turbid waters of the floodplain. Following eclosion, the resulting yolk-sac larva is entirely dependent on its endogenous yolk reserves for nutritional support during the initial days post-hatching. This early developmental trajectory is tightly linked to the seasonal dynamics of the Amazonian floodplain, where spawning is timed to coincide with rising water levels that maximize the availability of suitable nursery habitat.

Embryonic development proceeds rapidly under controlled laboratory conditions. At a stable incubation temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the onset of exogenous feeding, marking the age at birth, occurs 7 days [ab = 7 days] after the initial hatching event. This relatively brief pre-feeding interval is consistent with the pattern observed in other migratory Prochilodontidae, where rapid yolk absorption is an adaptation to predictable seasonal flooding regimes that create ephemeral nursery habitats. After hatching, the free-swimming larva begins active foraging on microzooplankton following mouth opening, transitioning from lecithotrophic reliance to exogenous nutrition. The timing of this trophic switch is critical, as the small wet weight at first feeding of approximately 0.0004 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0004 grams] provides only a narrow window before the point of no return is reached.

Sexual maturation in this species is tightly linked to somatic growth rather than chronological age per se, with puberty occurring once individuals attain a total length at puberty of 19 centimeters [Lp = 19 centimeters]. Field studies using gonad histology indicate that fish below this threshold remain in an immature, previtellogenic state, while those exceeding it initiate gametogenesis during the rising limb of the annual hydrograph. The length-based trigger for puberty is thought to represent a reliable proxy for the accumulation of sufficient energy reserves to sustain the high metabolic demands of migration and spawning. Comparative data from a suite of syntopic characiforms show that Prochilodus nigricans matures at a relatively smaller proportion of its ultimate size than some congeners, a pattern that may reflect differences in the predictability of floodplain access and the associated risk of reproductive failure in any given year.

Adult body mass in this species reaches a maximum recorded wet weight of 1350 grams [Wwi = 1350 grams] for large, gravid females collected during the peak of the spawning run. This asymptotic mass is derived from length-weight relationships calibrated across multiple populations and is supported by specimens exceeding 45 cm [Li = 45 cm] in total length. In terms of longevity, mark-recapture studies conducted in the lower Amazon and its tributaries, where annual water temperatures average 27 °C [T = 27 °C], indicate a maximum lifespan of 8 years [am = 8 years]. This lifespan is consistent with that of other large-bodied Neotropical migratory fishes, which typically exhibit a lifespan on the order of several years before senescent decline in condition becomes apparent. The age structure of exploited populations suggests that few individuals survive beyond this maximum, though potential longevity in unexploited systems may be slightly greater.

Ecological interactions with the floodplain mosaic are central to the life history of Prochilodus nigricans. During the falling-water phase, sexually mature adults undertake upstream migrations toward headwater spawning grounds, where gamete release coincides with the rising waters of the subsequent wet season. The pelagic larvae and subsequently the actively growing larvae drift downstream into the floodplain lakes, which serve as critical nursery habitats rich in periphyton and detrital resources. The post-metamorphic juveniles and sub-adults then recruit into the main river channel, where they continue growing until they reach the size threshold for puberty.
